key_insight: Elementary teachers do more than adopt AI tools—they actively adapt, translate, and reshape them so they fit children’s needs, classroom routines, and learning goals. The paper highlights teacher “implementation work” as a critical factor in making conversational AI usable in real schools.
problem_solved: This paper addresses the gap between promising AI classroom tools and the practical realities of elementary school use. It examines how teachers make an AI-integrated curriculum workable, appropriate, and educationally meaningful for young students.
method: Studied three elementary teachers implementing an AI literacy curriculum with conversational AI tools.
Examined how teachers adjusted instructions, activities, pacing, and classroom management to suit their students and context.
Analyzed teachers’ lived implementation experiences to identify the kinds of adaptations needed for successful classroom integration.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this shows that model quality alone is not enough for educational deployment. Designing for schools requires supporting teachers with flexibility, explainability, and classroom-ready workflows that can be adapted locally.
visual_elements: A classroom workflow diagram showing where teachers modify the AI curriculum.
An icon-based timeline of implementation steps: plan, adapt, teach, reflect.
A comparison chart of ‘intended use’ vs. ‘teacher-adjusted use’ of the AI tool.
Illustrations of teacher, student, and AI interaction in an elementary classroom.
paper_title: Adapting for AI: How elementary teachers adjust their practices for an AI-integrated curriculum
paper_authors: Fasika Melese, Ruiyang Wu, Xinyue Cui, Joanna Perkins, Xiaoyi Tian
